**(Surah al-Takathur)**
*Eight verses, Meccan*

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾ ﴿until you visit the graves﴾

﷽

﴿Rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾ ﴿until you visit the graves﴾

In this passage there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-ilhā'* (diversion) means turning towards amusement (*al-lahw*). *Al-lahw* is turning towards what desire calls for. It is known that turning towards one thing requires turning away from others. For this reason the lexicographers said: "Fulan *alhānī* 'an kadhā," meaning, "so-and-so made me forget and occupied me." From this is the hadith: "When al-Zubayr heard the sound of thunder, he *lahā* from his speech," meaning he left it and turned away from it. Everything you abandon, you have *lahayta* (abandoned) it. *Al-takāthur* is boasting through abundance of wealth, status and virtues. It is said: *takāthara al-qawm takāthuran* when the people equal one another in the abundance of their virtues. Abu Muslim said: *al-takāthur* is a *tafā'ul* form derived from abundance (*al-kathrah*). A *tafā'ul* form occurs in one of three ways. It may denote an action between two parties, which is *mufā'alah*. It may denote the deliberate effort to perform an act, as when you say *takārahtu 'alā kadhā* ("I forced myself to do such-and-such") when you do it while disliking it; or *tabā'adtu 'ani al-amr* ("I made myself blind to the matter") when you feign blindness to it; or *taghāfaltu* ("I feigned heedlessness"). It may also denote the act itself, as when you say *tabā'adtu 'ani al-amr*, meaning "I went far from it." The word *al-takāthur* in this verse may bear the first two meanings. It may mean the *mufā'alah* sense, since how many pairs there are in which each says to the other: ﴿I am more than you in wealth and mightier in men﴾ (Al-Kahf: 34). It may also mean the deliberate striving for abundance, since the greedy person strives all his life to multiply his wealth. Know that boasting (*al-tafākhur*) and competing in abundance (*al-takāthur*) are one and the same thing. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿and boasting among yourselves﴾ (Al-Hadid: 20).

**The second issue:** Know that boasting only occurs when a person claims for himself some kind of happiness. The kinds of happiness are three:

The first is in the soul. The second is in the body. The third is what surrounds the body from outside. As for that which is in the soul,

[Page 73]

it is knowledge and noble character, and these are what is meant by His words, quoted about Abraham: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾ (Al-Shu'ara': 83). Through these one attains eternal life and everlasting happiness.

As for that which is in the body, it is health and beauty, and this is the second rank. As for what surrounds the body from outside, there are two kinds:

One is necessary, namely wealth and status. The other is not necessary, namely relatives and friends. This third rank that we have enumerated is in fact wanted entirely for the sake of the body, as evidenced by the fact that when one of his limbs suffers pain, he makes wealth and status a ransom for it.

As for bodily happiness, the virtuous among people want it only for the sake of spiritual happiness, for whoever is not physically sound is not free to acquire the lasting spiritual happinesses. Having understood this, we say: the rational person should direct his effort toward giving precedence to what is more important over what is less important. So boasting in wealth, status, helpers and relatives is boasting in the lowest of the ranks of the causes of happiness. Occupation with it prevents a person from attaining spiritual happiness through knowledge and action. This amounts to preferring the lowest ranks of happiness over the highest ranks, which is the reverse of what is obligatory and the opposite of the truth. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, censured them, saying: ﴿Rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾. It includes competing in number, in wealth, in status, in relatives, in helpers and in army, and in sum it includes competing in everything of this world and its pleasures and desires.

**The third issue:** His words ﴿ألهاكم﴾ (*alhākum*, "diverts you") may be a statement about them, or it may be an interrogative in the sense of rebuke and reproach, meaning *a-alhākum* ("Does it divert you?"), as was read in the recitations of ﴿أأنذرتهم﴾ (*a-andhartahum*, "Did you warn them?") and ﴿أنذرتهم﴾ (*andhartahum*, "You warned them"), and ﴿إذا كنا عظاما﴾ (*idhā kunnā 'iẓāman*, "When we are bones") and ﴿أئذا كنا عظاما﴾ (*a-idhā kunnā 'iẓāman*, "When we are bones?").

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates that competing in abundance and boasting are blameworthy. Reason indicates that competing in abundance and boasting in true happinesses is not blameworthy. An example of this is what is related of al-Abbas boasting that the provision of water (*al-siqayah*) was in his hand, and of Shaybah boasting that the key was in his hand, until 'Ali, peace be upon him, said: "And I cut off the snout of disbelief with my sword, so disbelief became mutilated, and you embraced Islam." This upset them, so the verse was revealed: ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims equal to [the faith of one who believes in Allah]?﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 19), and so on. We have mentioned in the explanation of His words: ﴿As for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ (Al-Duha: 11) that it is permissible for a person to take pride in his acts of obedience and in his good character if he thinks others will follow his example. Thus it is established that unrestricted competing is not blameworthy. Rather, competing in knowledge, obedience and praiseworthy character is what is praised, and it is the root of all good things. Therefore the *alif* and *lām* in *al-takāthur* are not for totality but for a known antecedent, namely competing in this world and its pleasures and attachments, for this is what prevents obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and servitude to Him. Since this is established in reason and agreed upon in all religions, it is entirely fitting that the definite article be placed upon it.

**The fifth issue:** Regarding the interpretation of the verse there are several views:

The first: ﴿Rivalry in numbers diverts you﴾. It is related that it was revealed concerning the clans of Banu Sahm and Banu 'Abd Manaf, who boasted about which of them was more numerous. The Banu 'Abd Manaf were more numerous, so the Banu Sahm said: "Count the total of our living and our dead together with the total of your living and your dead." They did so, and the Banu Sahm came out ahead, so the verse was revealed. This report agrees with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, because His words ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ indicate that this is a past event. It is as if He, exalted is He, is making them marvel at themselves and saying: "Suppose you are more than them in number; what good does that do?" Visiting (*al-ziyārah*) means coming to a place, and it happens for many purposes, the most important and most deserving of attention being softening the heart and removing love of this world. For contemplating graves produces that, as he, peace be upon him, said: "I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them, for in visiting them there is a reminder." Then you visited the graves, due to the hardness of heart and the absorption in love of this world. When this matter was reversed, Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it in the context of wonder.

The second view: the intended meaning is competing in wealth. They cited as evidence what Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir related from his father, that he, peace be upon him, used to recite ﴿Alhākum﴾ and said: "The son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth.' Do you have from your wealth anything except what you ate and so consumed, or what you wore and so wore out, or what you gave in charity and so sent forward?" As for His words ﴿until you visit the graves﴾, the meaning is "until you die." Visiting a grave is an expression for death. It is said of one who has died: "He visited his grave" and "He visited his tomb." Jarir said to al-Akhtal:

*"Abu Malik visited the graves, and so he became the basest of their visitors."*

meaning he died. The meaning of the verse then is: your greed to multiply your wealth has diverted you from obeying your Lord until death came to you while you were still in that state. It is said: understanding it in this way is problematic in two respects.

The first: a visitor is one who visits for an hour and then departs, whereas the dead remain in their graves, so how can it be said that he visited the grave?

The second: His words ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ are a report about the past, so how can it be taken to refer to the future?

The answer to the first question is that the visitor may stay, but he must eventually depart. Likewise, the people of the graves depart from them to the place of reckoning.

The answer to the second question has several aspects:

First: the intended meaning may be one who was close to death because of old age, and for this reason it is said of him that he is "on the edge of the grave."

Second: the report about those who preceded them is a warning to them, so it is like a report about them, because they were upon their way. An example is His words: ﴿and they kill the prophets﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 61).

Third: Abu Muslim said: Allah, exalted is He, speaks in this surah on the Day of Resurrection as a rebuke to the disbelievers, and by that time they had already visited graves.

The third view: ﴿Alhākum﴾ means the greed for wealth and the pursuit of increasing it, to the point that you withheld the financial rights until the time of death. Then you say in that state: "I bequeathed such-and-such for the sake of zakat, and such-and-such for the sake of the pilgrimage."

The fourth view: ﴿Rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾, so you do not turn toward the religion. Rather your hearts are as if they were stones that do not break at all except when you visit the graves. This is how your state should be, and it means that your share of your religion is that small measure of humbling yourselves. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾ (Al-A'raf: 10), meaning I am not content with you giving only this small measure of thanks.

**The sixth issue:** He, exalted is He, did not say ﴿Rivalry in worldly gain diverts you﴾ "from such-and-such." Rather He left it unspecified, because the unrestricted form is more eloquent in censure, since the mind goes in every direction with it, and so it includes everything the context can bear. That is: rivalry in worldly gain diverts you from the remembrance of Allah, from obligatory and recommended acts, and from knowledge, obedience, reflection and contemplation. Or we may say: if we look at what precedes this verse, the meaning is that rivalry in worldly gain diverts you from reflecting on the Calamity (*al-qāri'ah*) and from preparing for it before death. And if we look at what follows, the meaning is: rivalry in worldly gain diverts you, so that you forget the grave until you visit it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 102, verses 3–7:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, you will soon know.﴾ ﴿Again, nay, you will soon know.﴾ It is connected to what precedes it and to what follows it. As for the first connection, it is in the manner of rebuke and denial, meaning: the matter is not as these people imagine, that true happiness lies in abundance of numbers and children. As for its connection to what follows, it is in the sense of an oath, meaning: truly, you will soon know. However, [this knowledge comes] when the sinner becomes a penitent, the disbeliever becomes a Muslim, and the greedy becomes an ascetic. From this is the saying of al-Hasan: "Let not the multitude you see around you deceive you, for you will die alone, and you will be called to account alone." Its confirmation is: ﴿On the Day when a man will flee﴾ [80:34], ﴿And you will come to Us alone﴾ [19:80], ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you first﴾ [6:94], up to His saying: ﴿and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾ [6:94]. This prevents you from excessive pursuit of wealth. The scholars have mentioned several aspects regarding the repetition:

First: that it is for emphasis, and that it is a warning after a warning, just as you say to one who is being advised: "I am telling you, and again I am telling you: do not do it."

Second: that the first is at death, when it is said to him: "No good tidings," the second is in the questioning of the grave: "Who is your Lord?" and the third is at the Resurrection, when the caller calls: "So-and-so is wretched, with a wretchedness after which there is no happiness forever," and when it is said: ﴿And separate yourselves today﴾ [36:59].

Third: from al-Dahhak: "You will soon know," O disbelievers; "Again, nay, you will soon know," O believers. He used to recite it that way. Thus the first is a warning and the second a promise.

Fourth: that every person knows the ugliness of wrongdoing and lying, and the goodness of justice and truthfulness, but does not know the extent of their effects and consequences. Then He, Exalted, says: "You will soon know" with detailed knowledge, but detail admits of increase. Whenever an increase in pleasure occurs, knowledge increases; likewise in the case of punishment. So He divided this according to states: at direct witnessing it increases, then at resurrection, then at reckoning, then at entering Paradise and Hell. Hence the repetition occurred.

Fifth: that one of the two states is the punishment of the grave and the other is the punishment of the Resurrection, as it is related from Abu Dharr that he said: "I used to doubt the punishment of the grave, until I heard 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, say: 'This verse indicates the punishment of the grave.'" He said "then" (thumma) because between the two worlds and the two lives there is death.

﴿Nay, if you knew with certainty of knowledge﴾ ﴿you would surely see the Hellfire﴾ ﴿Again, you will surely see it with the eye of certainty.﴾ In this there are several issues:

First issue: They agree that the answer to "law" (lau) is omitted, and that the saying ﴿you would surely see the Hellfire﴾ is not the answer to "law." Two points indicate this:

One: what is the answer of "law" has a negation that is an affirmation and an affirmation that is a negation. If ﴿you will surely see the Hellfire﴾ were the answer to "law," this sight would have to not occur, and that is false, since this sight is certainly going to happen. If it is said: the intended sight is seeing it with the heart in this world, and that sight does not occur, we reply: abandoning the apparent meaning is contrary to the original principle.

The second: His saying ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about the bounty﴾ is information about a matter that will certainly take place, so coordinating it with what does not exist and does not occur is an ugliness in the composition. Know that omitting the answer in such a place is better. A man says to another: "If you did this" — meaning: "it would be such-and-such." God, Exalted, says: ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to keep the Fire off their faces or off their backs﴾ [21:39], and no answer came for it. And He said: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ [6:30]. Having understood this, we say: they have mentioned several aspects regarding the answer of "law":

First: al-Akhfash said: the answer is "what distracted you was the abundance [of worldly gain]."

Second: Abu Muslim said: "If you knew what is obligatory upon you, you would hold fast to it," or "If you knew for what purpose you were created, you would occupy yourselves with it."

Third: that He omitted the answer so that the imagination would go in every direction, and the awe would be greater; as if He said: "If you knew with certainty, you would do what cannot be described or fathomed, but you are misguided and ignorant." As for His saying ﴿you will surely see the Hellfire﴾, the lam indicates that it is the answer to an omitted oath, and the oath is for the emphasis of the warning, and that what they are threatened with is something in which there is no room for doubt; and He repeated it, joined by "then," to intensify the threat and add to the awe.

Second issue: God, Exalted, repeated the word "Nay," which is for restraint. The repetition is good because He follows it in each place with something different from what He followed the other place with, as if He, Exalted, said: "Do not do this, for by it you deserve such-and-such punishment; do not do this, for by it you incur another harm." This repetition is not disliked; rather, it is pleasing to them. Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, used to take the meaning of "Nay" in this place to mean "truly," as if it were said: "Truly: ﴿If you knew with certainty of knowledge﴾."

Third issue: regarding His saying ﴿certainty of knowledge﴾ there are two aspects:

One: its meaning is "certain knowledge," so the qualified noun is idafa-ed to the qualifier, as in His saying: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter﴾ [12:109], and as one says: "the great mosque" and "the first year."

The second: that certainty here is death, resurrection and the Rising, and death has been called certainty in His saying: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [15:99]. And because when these occur, certainty comes and doubt departs. So the meaning is: if you knew the knowledge of death and what a person encounters with it and after it in the grave and in the Hereafter, abundance and boasting would not have distracted you from the remembrance of God. A person may say: "I know such-and-such knowledge," meaning: I verify it; and "So-and-so knows the knowledge of medicine and the knowledge of calculation," since knowledges are of kinds, so it is fitting to say: "I knew the knowledge of such-and-such."

* * *

Fourth issue: Knowledge is among the strongest incentives to action. If the time of action is before a person, it is a promise and an admonition; but if it is after the time of action has passed, then it becomes regret and remorse. As it is mentioned that Dhu al-Qarnayn, when he entered the darknesses, found jewels (*kharaz*). Those who were with him took from those jewels, and when they came out of the darknesses they found them to be gems. Second: Abu Muslim said: "If you knew what is obligatory upon you, you would hold fast to it," or "If you knew for what purpose you were created, you would occupy yourselves with it."

Third: that He omitted the answer so that the imagination would go in every direction, and the awe would be greater; as if He said: "If you knew with certainty, you would do what cannot be described or fathomed, but you are misguided and ignorant." Second issue: God, Exalted, repeated the word "Nay," which is for restraint. One: its meaning is "certain knowledge," so the qualified noun is idafa-ed to the qualifier, as in His saying: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter﴾ [12:109], and as one says: "the great mosque" and "the first year."

* * *

Fourth issue: Knowledge is among the strongest incentives to action. If the time of action is before a person, it is a promise and an admonition; but if it is after the time of action has passed, then it becomes regret and remorse. As it is mentioned that Dhu al-Qarnayn, when he entered the darknesses, found jewels (*kharaz*). Those who were with him took from those jewels, and when they came out of the darknesses they found them to be gems. Then those who had taken were in grief, that is, because they had not taken more than they took; and those who had not taken were also in grief. Thus is the condition of the people of the Resurrection.

This implies that whoever does not abandon abundance and boasting does not have certainty. So woe to the scholar who is not an active practitioner, then woe to him.

Sixth issue: Regarding the repetition of the seeing there are several aspects:

First: it is also for emphasizing the threat, perhaps because the people disliked hearing threats, so it was repeated for that reason. The nun of emphasis requires that this seeing be compulsory, meaning: if you were left to your own opinion you would not see it, but you will be compelled to see it, whether you wish or not.

Second: the first seeing is from afar: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ [25:12], and His saying ﴿And Hellfire is made manifest to whoever sees﴾ [79:36]; and the second seeing is when they reach the edge of the Fire.

Third: the first seeing is upon arrival, and the second upon entering it. It has been said: this interpretation is not good, because He said ﴿Then you will surely be questioned﴾, and questioning occurs before entering.

Fourth: the first seeing is the promise, and the second is direct witnessing.

Fifth: that what is intended is "you will surely see the Hellfire" more than once, so mentioning seeing twice is an expression of the continuity and succession of the seeing, because they are abiding in the Fire. As if it were said to them as a warning: "If you today are doubting it and not believing in it, you will see it with a lasting, continuous sight, and your doubts will depart." This is like His saying: ﴿You will not see any disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful... return the sight twice﴾ [67:3–4], meaning: if you look at it again as much as you wish, you will not find any flaw; and He did not intend only twice. So likewise here. If it is said: what is the benefit of specifying the second seeing with certainty? We say: because in the first time they saw only a blaze, and in the second time they saw the pit itself, how one falls into it, and the harmful creatures in it. Without doubt this seeing is clearer. The wisdom in moving from the less clear knowledge to the clearer is a consequence of abandoning reflection, because they used to limit themselves to conjecture and did not seek more.

Seventh issue: The reading of the majority is *latarawunna* with an open *ta*, and it is also read with a *damma* from *ra'aytuhu al-shay'* (I showed him the thing), meaning that they will be brought to it and will see it. This reading is transmitted from Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i, as if they intended *latarawunnaha fatarawnaha* (you will surely be shown it, and you will see it); for this reason the second was read *thumma latarawunnaha* with an open *ta*. In the reading of the majority, the second is a repetition for emphasis and for the other benefits we have enumerated. Know that the reading of the majority is preferable for two reasons:

The first: al-Farra' said: the reading of the majority is more like the speech of the Arabs, because it is an intensification, and it is not fitting that the Jahim be its object.

The second: Abu 'Ali said: the meaning of ﴿you will surely see the Hellfire﴾ is "you will surely see the punishment of the Hellfire." If that is so, the threat concerns seeing its punishment, not seeing it itself. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿when they see the punishment﴾ [2:165], and His saying: ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment﴾ [16:85]. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 102, verse 8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bliss﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions.

The first issue: Who is it that will be asked about the bliss? Concerning this there are two opinions.

One of them, which is the more apparent, is that they are the disbelievers. Al-Hasan said: "Only the people of the Fire will be asked about the bliss." Two things support this:

The first is what is reported: when this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, have you considered a meal I ate with you in the house of Abu al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihan, of barley bread, meat, unripe dates and sweet water? Will that be among the bliss about which we are asked?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That applies only to the disbelievers." Then he recited: ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba': 17].

The second is that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates what we have mentioned. This is because the disbelievers were diverted by competition in worldly wealth and boasting of its pleasures from obedience to God Exalted and from occupying themselves with thanking Him. So God Exalted will ask them about these things on the Day of Resurrection, until He shows them that what they thought to be the cause of their happiness was in fact among the greatest causes of their misery in the Hereafter.

The second opinion is that it is general, applying to both the believer and the disbeliever. They argued with hadiths. Abu Hurayra reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The first thing a servant will be asked about on the Day of Resurrection concerning bliss will be that it will be said to him: Did We not make your body healthy and give you to drink of cold water?" Mahmud ibn Labid said: When this surah was revealed, they said: "O Messenger of God, about which bliss will we be asked? Only water and dates are ours, and our swords are on our shoulders, and the enemy is present. About which bliss will we be asked?" He said: "That will come to pass." It is also reported from Umar that he said: "About which bliss will we be asked, O Messenger of God, when we have been driven from our homes and our wealth?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wakes up secure in his dwelling, healthy in his body, and has the food of his day, it is as if the whole world has been gathered for him." It is also reported that a young man embraced Islam in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger of God taught him the surah Alhakum (At-Takathur). Then the Messenger of God married him to a woman. When he entered upon her and saw the great provision and abundant bliss, he went out and said: "I do not want that." The Prophet (ﷺ) asked him about it, and he said: "Did you not teach me: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bliss﴾? I cannot bear the answer to that."

[Page 78]

From Anas: when the verse was revealed, a needy man stood up and said: "Is there any of the favour upon me?" He said: "The shade, the sandals, and cold water." The most famous report on this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out one night to the mosque, and he had not stayed long before Abu Bakr came, and he said: "What brought you out, O Abu Bakr?" He said: "Hunger." He said: "By God, nothing brought me out but what brought you out." Then Umar entered and said the same. He said: "Get up, let us go to the house of Abu al-Haytham." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) knocked on the door and greeted three times, but no one answered. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned away, and his wife came out calling: "We heard your voice, but we wanted you to increase your greeting." He said something good to her. Then she said: "May my father and mother be your ransom. Abu al-Haytham has gone out to fetch sweet water for us." Then she set about a sa' of barley, ground it and baked it. Abu al-Haytham returned, slaughtered a young goat, and brought them fresh dates. They ate and drank, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is of the bliss about which you will be asked." It is also reported: "The feet of a servant will not move until he is asked about four things: about his life, how he spent it; his youth, how he wore it out; his wealth, from where he earned it and how he spent it; and his knowledge, what he did with it." It is also reported from Mu'adh from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed the servant will be asked on the Day of Resurrection even about the kohl of his eyes, the crumbs of clay with his finger, and touching the garment of his brother."

Know that the better view is to say: the questioning is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever. But the questioning of the disbeliever is a rebuke (tawbikh), because he abandoned gratitude; and the questioning of the believer is a questioning of honour (tashrif), because he was grateful and obedient.

* * *

The second issue: They mentioned several aspects regarding the bliss about which one is asked.

The first: it is reported that it is five things: satisfaction of the bellies, cold drink, the pleasure of sleep, shade of dwellings, and balance of creation.

The second: Ibn Mas'ud said: it is security, health and leisure.

The third: Ibn Abbas said: it is health and all the delights of food and drink.

The fourth: some said: benefiting from the perception of hearing and sight.

The fifth: al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the lightening of the laws and the facilitation of the Qur'an.

The sixth: Ibn Umar said: it is cold water.

The seventh: al-Baqir said: it is well-being. It is also reported from Jabir al-Ju'fi who said: I entered upon al-Baqir and he said: "What do the people of interpretation say about His saying: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bliss﴾?" I said: "They say: shade and cold water." He said: "If you brought someone into your house and seated him in shade and gave him cold water, would you consider yourself to be doing him a favour?" I said: "No." He said: "God is more exalted than to feed His servant and give him to drink and then ask him about it." I said: "What is its interpretation?" He said: "The bliss is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by whom God bestowed favour upon this world, rescuing them through him from error. Have you not heard His saying: ﴿Certainly God conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164]," and so on.

The eighth view: they will only be asked about what exceeds what is necessary of food, clothing and shelter.

The ninth, which is the better: it must be taken to cover all blessings. This is supported by several aspects:

The first: the alif and lam (definite article) indicate comprehensiveness (istighraq).

The second: it is not more appropriate to restrict the word to some of them rather than the rest, especially since the evidence has shown that what is required from the benefits of this world is that the servant occupy himself with the worship of God Exalted.

The third: He Exalted said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, and what is meant by it is all blessings: from splitting the sea, deliverance from Pharaoh, and the sending down of manna and quail. So it is likewise here.

The fourth: the complete bliss is like a single thing that has parts and limbs, so when bliss is mentioned, all of it is included, just as theriac is the name of a compound made of many medicines, so when theriac is mentioned, all of it is included.

Know that blessings are of several kinds: some are apparent and some hidden, some are connected and some separate, and some are religious and some worldly. We have already mentioned the kinds of felicities according to genus in the commentary on the beginning of this surah. As for enumerating them according to type and individual, it is impossible, as He Exalted said: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. Seek help in knowing God's favours upon you regarding the health of your body from physicians, yet they are the most heedless of creation. And regarding knowing God's favours upon you through the creation of the heavens and the stars, from astrologers, yet they are the people most ignorant of the Creator. And regarding knowing God's sovereignty from kings, yet they are the most ignorant of creation.

As for what is reported from Ibn Umar that it is cold water, its meaning is that it is included in this; perhaps he singled it out for mention because it is the most easily available of existing things and the most precious when lacking. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Sammak to al-Rashid: "Consider: if you were in need of a sip of water in a desert, would you give half your kingdom for it? And if you were choking on it, would you give half your kingdom? And if your urine were blocked, would you give your whole kingdom? So do not be deceived by a kingdom whose single sip of water is worth twice its value." Or because the people of the Fire seek water more intensely than they seek anything else; He Exalted said: ﴿Pour out on us some water﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. Or because the surah was revealed concerning the affluent, and they are the ones who are specially associated with cold water and shade.

The truth is that the questioning is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever, about all bliss, whether it is among what is indispensable [or not]. This is not so because all of that must be directed to obedience to God and not to disobedience, so the questioning falls upon the whole. This is confirmed by what is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "The feet of a servant will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about four things: about his life, how he spent it; about his youth, how he wore it out; about his wealth, from where he acquired it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge, what he did with it." So all bliss from God Exalted is included in what he (ﷺ) mentioned.

* * *

The third issue: They differed about where this questioning will take place.

The first view: this questioning will only occur at the place of reckoning. If it is said: this is not correct, because He Exalted informed that this questioning comes after witnessing Hell by His saying: ﴿Then﴾, while the place of questioning precedes the witnessing of Hell? We say: what is meant by His saying ﴿Then﴾ is: then I inform you that you will be asked on the Day of Resurrection. It is like His saying: ﴿Freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan of near relationship, or a poor man in misery; then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 14–17].

The second view: when they enter the Fire they will be asked about the bliss as a rebuke to them, as He said: ﴿Every time a company is cast into it, its keepers will ask them﴾ [al-Mulk: 8], and He said: ﴿What led you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42]. There is no doubt that the coming of the Messenger is a favour from God, so they were asked about it after entering the Fire. Or it may be said: when they are in the Blazing Fire and witness it, it will be said to them: this punishment has befallen you only because in the abode of the world you occupied yourselves with bliss away from the deeds that would have saved you from this Fire. Had you spent your lives in obedience to your Lord, you would today be among those who are saved and who triumph with ranks. Thus that would be a questioning by the angels about their bliss in the world. And God, Glorified and Exalted, knows best. May God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
